Question five. How do you A B test an LLM feature? The usual machinery, with four adjustments. Randomize by user, and keep it sticky across sessions, so nobody sees both arms. Expect more variance: the same input gives different outputs, so the treatment is a distribution. Size the test from an A A test, both arms identical, or from a pilot. Pin the model version. A provider can update a model under the same name mid-test, and then the treatment changes halfway through. Log the version on every request. And add guardrails: latency at the ninety-fifth percentile, called p ninety-five, cost per active user, refusals, and hand-offs to a human. Better but twice as slow can still be a loss. Next, the model as the measuring tool itself.

Question six. You use an LLM to sort a million support tickets. How do you report the share that are complaints? Not as the share it labels complaints, because its errors bias that number. Check it on a hand-labeled sample: it catches ninety percent of real complaints, and wrongly flags five percent of everything else. Twenty percent come back labeled complaints. But five percent of the large majority that aren't complaints adds up to a lot of false alarms. Correct for both errors, and the share is about seventeen point six percent. That's the Rogan-Gladen estimator. Report its interval too, since both error rates came from a sample. And the last of the seven: the assistant's own work.
